title: Falling for fake news: Investigating the consumption of news via social media
screen_reason: CHI 2018 paper with two parts. Part one is a descriptive online survey of 309 UK internet users (May 2017) about news consumption via social media, which reports two self-reported encounter shares: 37% had come across a news story they believed to be true and later realised was exaggerated, inaccurate or blatantly false, and 46% had come across a news item they immediately identified as fake. Both are RECALL rows (recall_subtype exposure). Part two, a think-aloud task in which participants hunted for fake posts in a fabricated Facebook feed, is a discernment study and yields no prevalence estimate.

estimates.notes: Same country x platform cell as the 37% row and a different encounter definition, hence definition_variant true, though the two are not nested: one counts encounters that fooled the respondent, the other encounters that did not. Borderline because satire recognised as satire is the dominant case here, and satire that the reader knows is satire is a weak instance of misinformation exposure. The paper does not report how much the two groups overlap, so the two values cannot be summed.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) news-consumption frequencies (65% accessed news via their Facebook feeds at least once a day, 80% online news, 34% television daily, 20% obtained 'most' of their news via Facebook) - media use, not misinformation; (b) topic preferences (breaking news 69%, politics 45%, international 42%, entertainment 40%); (c) 'only 55% believed that the headline accurately matched the content' among those who read an article - a perception of headline-content match, closer to a quality judgement than to misinformation exposure, and its denominator is the unstated subset who read articles; (d) the entire second study (13 news posts in a fabricated 'Leo Porter' Facebook feed, think-aloud fake-spotting) - a discernment/judgement task with researcher-chosen stimuli, so any accuracy rate from it is not a prevalence estimate; (e) all figures quoted in Related Work from other sources (66% of UK residents use social media, two thirds of US Facebook users get news there, 29% read or shared news on Facebook in the last week) - cited from elsewhere. For a human: this is a 2017 student-heavy snowball sample of 309 with no reported response rate, so precision on the 37% and 46% is weak; and the survey item wording for both figures is paraphrased in the paper rather than reproduced, so the exact question stems are unavailable.

rob.design: Two-part study. Survey: descriptive online questionnaire advertised through an online survey tool and snowballed from institutional mailing lists, 309 UK respondents completing in May 2017 (41.1% male, 55.7% female; 70.4% aged 18-25; 71% students). No sampling frame, no response rate, no weighting. Items on news channels, news types, verification behaviour and encounters with stories later found untrue; the authors avoided the term 'fake news' in the encounter items and used Rubin's typology (satire, hoax, serious fabrication) instead. Main study: 13 news posts, mixing real and fake, embedded in a fabricated Facebook profile; participants thought aloud while finding the fake news, analysed qualitatively.
